intro: Every mat, ring and gym has a door. Someone decides who may walk through it. For much of history, those decisions shut many people out. Women were kept off the mat in judo, boxing, wrestling and sumo. Governments also used the gym, putting national arts into school timetables to shape young citizens.

This unit follows both stories. You will read a 37-word federal law from 1972, a 1959 medal taken from a judo champion, and Olympic lists that added women's names from 1924 to 2012. You will also see Japan's Ministry of Education require judo or kendo in 1931, China name its arts guoshu and then wushu, and South Korea make taekwondo its national sport by law in 2018.

By the end, you can explain who opened doors and when. You can name the laws, bodies and dates behind each change. You can also weigh a hard question: when a state puts an art into the gym, is it building health, a nation, or both?
bigQuestion: Who decides who may stand on the mat, and how have laws and governments changed the answer?

test.q: In what year was Title IX signed?
test.why: President Richard Nixon signed the Education Amendments of 1972, including Title IX, on June 23, 1972.

test.q: Which combat sport first opened Olympic medal events to women?
test.why: Women's foil fencing joined the Paris Games in 1924, decades before the other combat sports.

test.q: What did Rusty Kanokogi organize in 1980?
choices: The first IHSA girls wrestling finals
The first Women's World Judo Championships
The first women's Olympic boxing event
test.why: Kanokogi raised money for and organized the first women's world judo championships in New York City.

test.q: Who was the first woman to hold judo's tenth degree?
test.why: USA Judo awarded Keiko Fukuda tenth degree in 2011.

test.q: When did the IHSA crown its first boys wrestling champions and hold its first girls finals?
test.why: IHSA records list the first boys champions in 1937 and the first girls state finals in 2022.

choices: An Olympic sport in which medals do not count
A court case about a ban
test.why: Women's judo was a demonstration event in 1988, so its medals were not official.

test.q: What was the Dai Nippon Butokukai?
choices: A national martial arts body founded in Kyoto in 1895
test.why: The Butokukai was founded in Kyoto in 1895 and set standards for Japan's martial arts.

test.q: What did Japan's Ministry of Education do in 1931?
choices: Made judo or kendo required for boys in middle schools
test.why: In 1931 judo or kendo became compulsory for boys in middle schools.

test.q: Why was the Butokukai dissolved in 1946?
choices: The Occupation tied it to wartime militarism
test.why: The Allied Occupation worked to remove militarism, and the government-run Butokukai was dissolved.
Guoshu means national art, the Nationalist government's name for Chinese martial arts.

test.q: Which Chinese body was founded in 1958?
test.why: The Chinese Wushu Association was founded in 1958 under the People's Republic.

choices: Early martial arts schools in Seoul after the mid-1940s
test.why: Kwan means hall; these Seoul schools grew into taekwondo.

test.q: How did South Korea's government use taekwondo in the 1960s?
choices: As a national symbol shown abroad by troops and teams
test.why: The Park government backed taekwondo, and troops and demonstration teams showed it abroad.

test.q: How did Japan's 2012 school rule differ from its 1931 rule?
choices: In 2012 budo was taught as culture in PE for all students, not as preparation for war
test.why: The 1931 rule served a militarizing state; the 2012 rule placed budo in junior high PE as national culture.

test.q: Why was the 2018 UNESCO listing of ssireum a first?
choices: It turned ssireum into an Olympic sport
North and South Korea asked together to honor a shared folk wrestling
It came from Japan's Ministry of Education
test.why: The two Koreas made their first joint UNESCO request to honor ssireum as shared heritage.

write.prompt: Who has decided who may stand on the mat? Choose two cases from this unit, such as Title IX (1972), the 1993 Dallas Malloy case, Japan's 1931 school rule, or South Korea's 2018 law. Name each document or record and its date, explain what it decided, and argue whether a law, a governing body or a person mattered most.
tips: Name each law, rule book or body with its date.
Say who made each decision: a government, a federation or a court.
Compare the two cases before you judge them.
Use unit words such as sanctioned, compulsory and weight class.
Describe each tradition with respect for the people who practice it.
